advances: Complete supports built from private-group leaves have an absolute original cubic lower bound for every affine field even when each neutral coordinate belongs to as many as two groups, provided the explicit inverse-size budget holds. This includes independent arbitrary fields on every neutral coordinate. The disjoint-group specialization obstructs bounded retained parity-energy capacity: its particular low field has vanishing original core mass and weighted core coverage, unbounded core cardinality relative to the Boolean cube, and capacity of order at least \(m2^k\) for every subset of original mass at least one half, while both actual original cubics diverge after multiplication by \(8^{k+1}\). This is a strategy calibration and does not settle the locked mixed-integer statement.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The construction, lattice completeness, arbitrary-field composition, particular-field mass and cardinality estimates, retained-capacity obstruction, and divergent actual moments are proved above. The three declared accepted predecessors are used only with the explicit support, field, normalization, and embedding maps given in the statement and proof.
proof:
We first prove the construction and its exact lattice geometry. Every generator of \(P\) belongs to \([0,2]^k\), has at most one active two and at most one neutral two. If a coordinate of a point in \(P\) equals two, every generator with positive coefficient in any convex representation has that coordinate equal to two. It follows that a lattice point of \(P\) has at most one active two and at most one neutral two.

If a lattice point has an active two at index \(i\), all representing generators have an active two at \(i\). Their other active coordinates are binary. An integral value zero or one in any such coordinate fixes that bit in every generator with positive coefficient. Thus exactly one family \(E_q\), with \(q=(b,i)\), occurs. Every member of this family has neutral coordinate sum on \(G_q\) at least two. If the lattice point has a neutral two, its index must lie in \(G_q\), and every other neutral coordinate is binary, so it belongs to \(E_q\). Otherwise its neutral coordinates are binary and it belongs to \(F_q\). This argument does not require disjoint groups.

A remaining lattice point either has neither kind of two and lies in \(B_k\), or has Boolean active coordinates and precisely one neutral two, with all other neutral coordinates binary. Define \(R\) to be the set of the latter points of \(D\). This proves one inclusion of the decomposition (1), with \(R\) as asserted.

Conversely, \(B_k\cup E\) consists of generators. For a point in \(F_q\), choose distinct indices \(h,l\in G_q\) at which its neutral vector has two ones. Replace these entries respectively by \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\), leaving every other coordinate fixed. The resulting two points lie in \(E_q\), and their midpoint is the original point. Hence \(F\subseteq P\). An active vector \(b+2e_i\) uniquely determines \((b,i)\); presence or absence of a neutral two distinguishes \(E_q\) and \(F_q\). These sets are disjoint from \(B_k\) and \(R\). This proves all disjointness and the exact decomposition (1). Since \(B_k\cup E\subseteq D\subseteq P\), their convex hulls equal \(P\), proving completeness. Containment of \(B_k\) gives full dimension.

The actual one-step core is \(D_1=B_k\mathbin{\dot\cup}F\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\). It is complete. Indeed an integer point of \(\operatorname{conv}(D_1)\) lies in \(D\). If it had two coordinates equal to two, extremality of the value two in \([0,2]\) would force every point with positive coefficient in its convex representation by \(D_1\) to have both coordinates equal to two. That contradicts membership in \(D_1\). Thus it belongs to \(D_1\), proving \(\operatorname{conv}(D_1)\cap\mathbb Z^k=D_1\).

For any integer \(a\ge2\), write
$$
\begin{aligned}
E_a^{\mathrm{leaf}}&=\left\lbrace u\in\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^a:
\#\lbrace h:u_h=2\rbrace=1\right\rbrace,\\
S_a&=E_a^{\mathrm{leaf}}\cup\left\lbrace u\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^a:
\sum_hu_h\ge2\right\rbrace.
\end{aligned}
$$
These are exactly \(E_\ell,S_\ell\) of accepted fact 128f3b41bb80c5e7 at \(\ell=a\). For clarity, completeness here also follows directly. A lattice point in \(\operatorname{conv}(E_a^{\mathrm{leaf}})\) either has a coordinate equal to two, in which case all its other coordinates are binary, or is Boolean. Its coordinate sum is at least two. Thus it lies in \(S_a\). Every Boolean member of \(S_a\) is the midpoint of two spike members obtained from two of its ones by the replacements \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\). Hence \(\operatorname{conv}(S_a)=\operatorname{conv}(E_a^{\mathrm{leaf}})\) and \(S_a\) is complete. Products with Boolean cubes are complete because the convex hull of a product is the product of convex hulls, as follows by multiplying convex combination coefficients in the two factors.

Fix now an arbitrary original field \(\beta=(\gamma,\eta)\), with positive active activities \(\rho_i=\exp(-\gamma_i)\) and neutral activities \(a_h=\exp(-\eta_h)\). For each \(q=(b,i)\), choose a bijection \(\sigma_q:\lbrace1,\ldots,L\rbrace\to\lbrace1,\ldots,L\rbrace\) whose first \(n_q\) values enumerate \(G_q\). Its residual support in these ordered coordinates is exactly
$$
R_q=S_{n_q}\times\lbrace0,1\rbrace^{L-n_q}.
\tag{7}
$$
The exact affine injection is \(\Phi_q(u)=(b+2e_i,t)\), where \(t_{\sigma_q(r)}=u_r\) for every \(1\le r\le L\). Its image is \(C_q\). Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_q^{\mathrm{res}}&=\sum_{u\in R_q}\prod_{r=1}^L a_{\sigma_q(r)}^{u_r},
\qquad \lambda_q=\frac{\left(\prod_{j=1}^m\rho_j^{b_j+2\mathbf1_{j=i}}\right)Z_q^{\mathrm{res}}}{Z},\\
\pi_q(u)&=\frac{\prod_{r=1}^L a_{\sigma_q(r)}^{u_r}}{Z_q^{\mathrm{res}}}\quad(u\in R_q).
\end{aligned}
$$
The disjoint decomposition gives the exact identities
$$
\lambda_q=p(C_q),\qquad
\sum_q\lambda_q=p\left(\bigcup_q C_q\right),\qquad
p_{\Phi_q(u)}=\lambda_q\pi_q(u)\quad(u\in R_q).
\tag{8}
$$
Thus the \(\lambda\)'s are original masses, and the auxiliary conditional laws in (8) are explicitly normalized restrictions of the original law.

Use the same definitions of depth and reflection cubic for each \(\pi_q\) on \(R_q\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^{L+1}\). A containing original halfspace pulls back under \(u\mapsto(\Phi_q(u),0)\) to a containing residual halfspace if its restriction has nonzero normal. If the restricted normal is zero, containment of the center makes its restriction the whole residual space. Its conditional mass is then one, which is at least the conditional depth. Therefore, for every residual center,
$$
\tau_p((\Phi_q(u),0))\ge\lambda_q\tau_{\pi_q}((u,0)).
$$
Every ordered reflected residual pair maps to an original reflected pair, with its minimum probability multiplied by exactly \(\lambda_q\). Summing over the disjoint center sets proves
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)&\ge\sum_q\lambda_q^4M_3(\pi_q),\\
T(p)&\ge\sum_q\lambda_q^4T(\pi_q).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
$$
This proves the fourth-power mass factors for actual depths and actual reflection sums, including every embedding and zero-normal case. No factorization of halfspace depths is asserted.

We will also use a direct comparison valid for every finite positive probability law in any affine rank. About any center \(c\), distinct unordered non-diagonal reflected pairs have disjoint endpoints, all different from \(c\). Every closed halfspace containing \(c\) contains at least one endpoint of each pair, since otherwise their midpoint is strictly outside. Consequently
$$
\tau_p((c,0))\ge p_c+\frac12\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D,\ x\ne y\\x+y=2c}}\min(p_x,p_y)
=\frac{p_c+s_p(c)}2\ge\frac{s_p(c)}2,
\qquad M_3(p)\ge\frac18T(p).
\tag{10}
$$
The same proof applies to every auxiliary conditional law. Always \(\tau_p((c,0))\ge p_c\) and \(s_p(c)\ge p_c\).

For a normalized Boolean product law with activities \(u_1,\ldots,u_d>0\), its sum of fourth powers is
$$
\prod_{h=1}^d\frac{1+u_h^4}{(1+u_h)^4}\ge8^{-d}.
\tag{11}
$$
Indeed \((1+u)^4\le8(1+u^4)\) by convexity of the fourth power.

First suppose the actual core mass \(\alpha\ge1/4\). On its complete support \(D_1\), use the normalized restriction \(\pi_1(x)=w_x/W_1\). Apply the final one-step assertion of accepted fact f27ee487069e27e7 with its integer dimension \(k\), support \(D_1\), embedding \(D_1\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+1}\), and original field \(\beta\). Its occupied parity count is at most \(2^k\), so both conditional cubics are at least \(1/(512\,8^k)\). The exact relation is \(p_x=\alpha\pi_1(x)\) on \(D_1\). Restricting a containing halfspace to this support and restricting reflected pairs gives the same fourth-power comparison as (9), hence
$$
M_3(p),\ T(p)\ge\frac{\alpha^4}{512\,8^k}\ge2^{-14}8^{-(k+1)},
$$
which implies (2).

Assume henceforth \(\alpha<1/4\). All points outside the core lie in \(E\), so \(p(E)=1-\alpha>3/4\) and \(\sum_q\lambda_q>3/4\). Call a label \(q\) good if all its private activities \(a_h\), \(h\in G_q\), belong to \([1/2,2]\), and bad otherwise. Good or bad cells therefore have total original mass at least \(1/4\).

For a good cell, apply accepted fact 128f3b41bb80c5e7 with its \(\ell=n_q\), \(f=L-n_q\), and its ambient \(N=L+1\). Its private activities are \(r_j=a_{\sigma_q(j)}\) for \(1\le j\le n_q\), and its arbitrary free activities are \(t_h=a_{\sigma_q(n_q+h)}\) for \(1\le h\le L-n_q\). Its support and normalized probability are respectively (7) and \(\pi_q\). The coordinate permutation and fixed active translation have already been handled in (9). This yields, for each good label,
$$
M_3(\pi_q),\ T(\pi_q)\ge2^{-38}n_q^2 8^{-(L+1)}.
\tag{12}
$$
If the good cells have mass \(\Lambda_{\mathrm g}=\sum_{q\text{ good}}\lambda_q\ge1/4\), Hölder gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Lambda_{\mathrm g}
&=\sum_{q\text{ good}}(\lambda_q^4n_q^2)^{1/4}n_q^{-1/2}\\
&\le\left(\sum_{q\text{ good}}\lambda_q^4n_q^2\right)^{1/4}
\left(\sum_{q\text{ good}}n_q^{-2/3}\right)^{3/4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
By the assumed budget \(\sum_q n_q^{-2/3}\le2^m\),
\(\sum_{q\text{ good}}\lambda_q^4n_q^2\ge\Lambda_{\mathrm g}^4/8^m\ge2^{-8}8^{-m}\). Equations (9) and (12) give
$$
M_3(p),\ T(p)\ge2^{-46}8^{-(m+L+1)}=2^{-46}8^{-(k+1)}.
\tag{13}
$$

For the remaining case, suppose bad cells have mass \(\Lambda_{\mathrm b}\ge1/4\), and let \(J\ge1\) be their number. Choose one witness index \(h_q\in G_q\) with \(a_{h_q}\notin[1/2,2]\) for each bad label, and let \(W\) be the set of distinct chosen indices. Incidence at most two gives
$$
|W|\ge J/2,\qquad \sum_{q\text{ bad}}|W\cap G_q|\le2|W|.
\tag{14}
$$
Every coordinate of \(W\) has activity outside \([1/2,2]\), regardless of which cell supplied it.

For arbitrary activities on the private factor \(S_{n_q}\), apply the final one-step assertion of accepted fact f27ee487069e27e7, with its support \(D=S_{n_q}\), its integer dimension \(k=n_q\), its field \((\eta_{\sigma_q(1)},\ldots,\eta_{\sigma_q(n_q)})\), its embedding \(S_{n_q}\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_q+1}\), and its normalized probability
$$
\pi_q^{\mathrm{leaf}}(u)=\frac{\prod_{r=1}^{n_q}a_{\sigma_q(r)}^{u_r}}{\sum_{v\in S_{n_q}}\prod_{r=1}^{n_q}a_{\sigma_q(r)}^{v_r}}.
$$
Completeness was proved above, and the private support has at most one two per point. The occupied parity count is at most \(2^{n_q}\). Therefore
$$
T(\pi_q^{\mathrm{leaf}})\ge\frac1{512\,8^{n_q}}.
\tag{15}
$$
This use of the accepted fact concerns its original normalized law on the private support; (8) states its exact relation, through the Boolean product factor, to the original full-support probabilities.

Set \(\mathcal G(u)=8(1+u^4)/(1+u)^4\). This scalar function satisfies
$$
\mathcal G(u)\ge1\quad(u>0),\qquad \mathcal G(u)=\mathcal G(1/u),\qquad
\mathcal G'(u)=\frac{32(u^3-1)}{(1+u)^5}.
$$
Consequently for \(u\notin[1/2,2]\),
$$
\mathcal G(u)\ge\mathcal G(2)=\mathcal G(1/2)=\frac{136}{81}>\frac32.
\tag{16}
$$
The private/free product law for \(\pi_q\) gives an exact reflection identity. Its free probability is
\(b_z=\prod_{r=n_q+1}^L\frac{a_{\sigma_q(r)}^{z_{r-n_q}}}{1+a_{\sigma_q(r)}}\), and \(\pi_q((u,z))=\pi_q^{\mathrm{leaf}}(u)b_z\). If Boolean endpoints \(v,v'\) reflect about a Boolean center \(z\), then each coordinate forces \(v=v'=z\). It follows that
$$
s_{\pi_q}((c,z))=b_zs_{\pi_q^{\mathrm{leaf}}}(c),
\qquad
T(\pi_q)=T(\pi_q^{\mathrm{leaf}})
\prod_{h\notin G_q}\frac{1+a_h^4}{(1+a_h)^4}.
$$
For a bad label \(q\), put \(d_q=|W\setminus G_q|\). These \(d_q\) distinct biased witness coordinates are free Boolean coordinates of \(R_q\). Equations (15) and (16) imply
$$
T(\pi_q)\ge\frac{(3/2)^{d_q}}{512\,8^L},
\qquad
M_3(\pi_q),\ T(\pi_q)\ge\frac{(3/2)^{d_q}}{512}\,8^{-(L+1)},
\tag{17}
$$
where the common bound uses (10). Call a bad label heavy if \(|W\cap G_q|>|W|/2\), and light otherwise. By (14), there are at most four heavy labels, since five such labels would make the sum exceed \(2|W|\). If their cells have total mass at least \(1/8\), Hölder gives
$$
\sum_{q\text{ heavy}}\lambda_q^4\ge\frac{(1/8)^4}{4^3}=2^{-18}.
$$
Using the bound (17) with \(d_q\ge0\) in (9) then gives
$$
M_3(p),\ T(p)\ge2^{-27}8^{-(L+1)}\ge2^{-46}8^{-(k+1)}.
$$

Otherwise the light bad cells have mass at least \(1/8\). Each such label satisfies
\(d_q\ge|W|/2\ge J/4\). There are at most \(J\) light labels, so Hölder gives \(\sum_{q\text{ light}}\lambda_q^4\ge2^{-12}/J^3\). To bound the exponential gain uniformly, let \(r=10/11\). The exact comparison \(2\cdot14641<3\cdot10000\) gives \((2/3)^{1/4}<r\). The geometric-series identity
$$
\sum_{a=1}^{\infty}a^3r^a=\frac{r(1+4r+r^2)}{(1-r)^4}
$$
follows by differentiating \(\sum_{a\ge0}r^a=(1-r)^{-1}\) three times and combining the expressions for \(a(a-1)(a-2)\), \(a(a-1)\), and \(a\). In particular,
$$
J^3(2/3)^{J/4}\le J^3r^J\le\sum_{a=1}^{\infty}a^3r^a
<6\cdot11^4=87846<2^{17}.
$$
Consequently (9) and (17) give
$$
M_3(p),\ T(p)\ge2^{-21}\frac{(3/2)^{J/4}}{J^3}\,8^{-(L+1)}
>2^{-38}8^{-(L+1)}\ge2^{-46}8^{-(k+1)}.
$$
This and the core and good cases prove (2). Empty good, bad, heavy, or light collections cause no exceptional case: every collection to which Hölder is applied has positive mass, hence is nonempty. In particular \(J\ge1\) and \(|W|>0\) in the bad case. Every field is allowed throughout.

We now verify that the particular disjoint-group construction satisfies every generic hypothesis, and prove (4)--(6) independently. Its group sizes are integers at least 16, and choosing disjoint groups gives incidence one and \(L\ge16Q\). Put \(v=4^{-2/3}\), so \(v<2/5\), since \(v^3=1/16<8/125=(2/5)^3\). Summing over the labels gives
$$
\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}n_q^{-2/3}
=\sum_{i=1}^m v^{2i}\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}(1+v^j)
<\frac47<1\le2^m.
$$
Indeed, for nonnegative \(x_j\) with sum \(s<1\), the finite expansion of \(\prod_j(1+x_j)\) is bounded by \(\sum_{r\ge0}s^r=1/(1-s)\): every squarefree monomial of degree \(r\) is included with coefficient at least one in \(s^r\). Here \(\sum_{j\ge1}v^j=v/(1-v)<2/3\), so each displayed product is less than three, while \(\sum_{i\ge1}v^{2i}<4/21\). This proves the required budget.

For disjoint groups there are no extra roots. If a lattice point of \(P\) has a neutral two at index \(h\), all representing generators have a two at \(h\). Its unique group determines a unique \(q\), so all these generators lie in \(E_q\), and their active coordinates are fixed to \(b+2e_i\). Thus the lattice point belongs to \(E_q\), excluding Boolean active coordinates. Hence \(R=\varnothing\), and (1) becomes the exact disjoint decomposition \(D=B_k\mathbin{\dot\cup}E\mathbin{\dot\cup}F\).

At the particular field (3), put \(c_q=4^{-(S_b+2i)}=1/n_q\) for \(q=(b,i)\), and put \(w_b=4^{-S_b}\). All original atoms of \(E_q\cup F_q\) have unnormalized weight \(c_q\), and Boolean atoms with active vector \(b\) have weight \(w_b\). Define
$$
f(a)=1-(a+1)2^{-a}\quad(a\ge16),
\qquad \mathcal B_m=\prod_{i=1}^m(1+4^{-i}).
$$
Counting the unique neutral two and then all other binary coordinates gives
$$
|E_q|=n_q2^{L-1},\qquad \sum_{x\in E_q}w_x=2^{L-1},
\qquad \sum_{x\in E}w_x=Q2^{L-1}.
\tag{18}
$$
Counting the binary vectors with at least two private ones gives
$$
|F_q|=2^L f(n_q),\qquad \sum_{x\in F_q}w_x=2^L c_q f(n_q).
\tag{19}
$$
The elementary product bound just proved, with \(\sum_{i=1}^m4^{-i}<1/3\), implies \(\mathcal B_m<3/2\). Direct summation over the active Boolean bits gives
$$
\sum_q c_q
=\sum_{i=1}^m16^{-i}\prod_{j\ne i}(1+4^{-j})
=\mathcal B_m\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{16^{-i}}{1+4^{-i}}
<\frac{\mathcal B_m}{15}<\frac1{10}.
\tag{20}
$$
The actual core is exactly \(D_1=B_k\mathbin{\dot\cup}F\). Hence
$$
\begin{aligned}
W_1&=2^L\left[\mathcal B_m+\sum_q c_q f(n_q)\right]\le\frac85\,2^L,\\
Z&=Q2^{L-1}+W_1,
\qquad Q2^{L-1}\le Z\le Q2^L.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
$$
For the final upper bound, \(Q\ge32\) and \(Q/2+8/5\le Q\). It follows that \(\alpha\le16/(5Q)\le4/Q\le1/8\).

The hypothetical full core separates into Boolean points, points with one active two, and points with one neutral two. Their weights sum respectively to \(\mathcal B_m2^L\), \(2^L\sum_qc_q\), and \(L\mathcal B_m2^{L-1}\). Therefore
$$
W_1^{\mathrm{full}}=2^L\left[\mathcal B_m(1+L/2)+\sum_qc_q\right]\ge L2^{L-1},
\qquad \delta\le\frac{16}{5L}\le\frac4L.
$$
For integers \(a\ge16\), \(a(a+1)\le2^a\): it holds at 16, and the ratio \(2^a/[a(a+1)]\) is nondecreasing for \(a\ge2\) because its consecutive ratio is \(2a/(a+2)\ge1\). Thus
$$
0\le Q-\sum_q f(n_q)=\sum_q(n_q+1)2^{-n_q}
\le\sum_q\frac1{n_q}<\frac1{10}.
$$
By (19), \(|D_1|/2^k=1+2^{-m}\sum_qf(n_q)\). Since \(Q=m2^{m-1}\), this proves the cardinality bounds in (4). The asserted limits follow from \(Q\to\infty\) and \(L\ge16Q\).

Fix an original parity class, specified by an active Boolean vector \(b\) and a neutral Boolean vector \(s\). Its Boolean atom has weight \(w_b\). Every other possible atom in it belongs to \(E_{b,i}\) or \(F_{b,i}\) for an index \(i\) with \(b_i=0\), and has weight \(c_{b,i}\). In \(E_{b,i}\), the neutral two can occur at precisely those indices \(h\in G_{b,i}\) for which \(s_h=0\), with the remaining neutral entries fixed by \(s\). There are at most \(n_{b,i}\) such atoms. Their total original probability is at most
$$
n_{b,i}\frac{c_{b,i}}Z=\frac1Z.
\tag{22}
$$
The represented energies in the class form a subset of
$$
\log Z+S_b\log4,
\qquad \log Z+(S_b+2i)\log4\quad(b_i=0).
\tag{23}
$$
Different indices \(i\) give distinct levels in that class. All distinct levels in (23) differ by at least \(2\log4\); Boolean and \(F\) atoms introduce no additional levels. Since \(\tanh((2\log4)/4)=3/5\), a retained class with \(d\) represented distinct levels contributes at least \(1+(3/5)(d-1)\ge(3/5)d\) to the canonical retained capacity.

Take any actual subset \(V\) with \(p(V)\ge1/2\). Since \(D\setminus E=D_1\), its retained \(E\) mass is at least \(1/2-\alpha\). Let \(R_V\) be the number of triples \((b,s,i)\) for which \(V\) contains at least one \(E_{b,i}\) atom of parity \((b,s)\). By (22), \(p(V\cap E)\le R_V/Z\), so \(R_V\ge Z(1/2-\alpha)\). Each triple is a distinct retained energy level within its own parity class, by (23). The preceding capacity estimate, \(\alpha\le1/8\), and (21) imply
$$
\kappa_{\mathrm{par},V}(p)\ge\frac35R_V\ge\frac9{40}Z,
\qquad
\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{par},V}(p)}{2^k}
\ge\frac9{40}\frac{Q2^{L-1}}{2^{m+L}}=\frac{9m}{160}.
$$
This proves (5) for every such \(V\), using the original probabilities throughout. The definition agrees with accepted fact 73f9d0102f4f4461 under the exact map in the statement; energy gaps are also unchanged if the retained probabilities are all multiplied by a common constant, although no such renormalization is used here.

Finally take \(i=m\) and \(b\) with all its other active bits equal to one and \(b_m=0\). Its private size is
$$
n=n_{b,m}=4^{m(m-1)/2+2m}=4^{m(m+3)/2},\qquad c_{b,m}=1/n.
$$
This size is maximal: for any other label \((b',i')\), \(S_{b'}\le m(m+1)/2-i'\), so \(S_{b'}+2i'\le m(m+1)/2+i'\le m(m+3)/2\). Let \(G\) be the chosen group. At least \(2^{L-1}\) neutral Boolean vectors have \(h=\sum_{j\in G}t_j\ge n/2\), because complementing their bits on \(G\) exchanges the values \(h\) and \(n-h\). Every associated point \(c=(b+2e_m,t)\) lies in \(F_{b,m}\), since \(n\ge16\), and has original probability \(1/(nZ)\).

For each ordered pair of distinct indices \((j,l)\) among the \(h\) private ones, replace these two neutral entries by \((2,0)\) to obtain an endpoint and by \((0,2)\) to obtain its reflected partner. Both endpoints lie in \(E_{b,m}\) and have original probability \(1/(nZ)\). Distinct ordered \((j,l)\) give distinct ordered endpoint pairs: the positions of the two at the first and second endpoints recover \(j\) and \(l\). Thus the full ordered reflection sum includes \(h(h-1)\) such terms. Since \(h\ge n/2\) and \(n\ge4\),
$$
s_p(c)\ge\frac{h(h-1)}{nZ}\ge\frac{n}{8Z},
\qquad \tau_p((c,0))\ge\frac{n}{16Z},
\tag{24}
$$
where the second inequality is the actual all-containing-halfspaces estimate (10). Summing over the at least \(2^{L-1}\) actual centers yields
$$
T(p)\ge\frac{2^{L-1}n^2}{512Z^4},
\qquad M_3(p)\ge\frac{2^{L-1}n^2}{4096Z^4}.
$$
Using \(Z\le Q2^L\) and \(k=m+L\) gives (6). Its common growing factor is
$$
\frac{n^2 8^m}{Q^4}=\frac{2^{2m^2+5m+4}}{m^4}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$
At every selected center, (24) and (21) also give
$$
2^N\tau_p((c,0))\ge\frac{2^{m+L+1}n}{16Q2^L}=\frac{n}{4m}.
$$
All reflection counts include the prescribed ordered terms and diagonal convention; additional original pairs can only increase the lower bounds. The proof used no tensorization of depth and no restriction on the rank of a support in its stated ambient embedding.
statement:
For integers \(m\ge1\) and \(L\ge2\), define the label set
$$
\mathcal Q=\left\lbrace(b,i):b\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m,\ 1\le i\le m,\ b_i=0\right\rbrace,
\qquad Q=|\mathcal Q|=m2^{m-1}.
$$
For every \(q\in\mathcal Q\), choose a group \(G_q\subseteq\lbrace1,\ldots,L\rbrace\) with size \(n_q\ge2\). Assume
$$
\#\lbrace q:h\in G_q\rbrace\le2\quad(1\le h\le L),
\qquad \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}n_q^{-2/3}\le2^m,
\qquad k=m+L,
\qquad N=k+1.
$$
Write a point of \(\mathbb R^k\) as \((y,t)\), with \(m\) active coordinates \(y\) and \(L\) neutral coordinates \(t\). Let \(B_k=\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k\). For each \(q=(b,i)\), define
$$
\begin{aligned}
E_q=\bigl\lbrace&(b+2e_i,t):\text{exactly one neutral coordinate equals two,}\\
&\text{its index lies in }G_q,\text{ and all other neutral coordinates are binary}\bigr\rbrace,\\
F_q=\left\lbrace(b+2e_i,t):t\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^L,\ \sum_{h\in G_q}t_h\ge2\right\rbrace,\\
E&=\bigcup_{q\in\mathcal Q}E_q,\qquad F=\bigcup_{q\in\mathcal Q}F_q,\\
P&=\operatorname{conv}(B_k\cup E),\qquad D=P\cap\mathbb Z^k.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here \(e_i\) is the active coordinate unit vector. With \(C_q=E_q\cup F_q\), one has the disjoint decomposition
$$
D=B_k\mathbin{\dot\cup}\coprod_{q\in\mathcal Q}(E_q\mathbin{\dot\cup}F_q)\mathbin{\dot\cup}R
=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^k
\subseteq\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^k.
\tag{1}
$$
Here \(R=D\setminus(B_k\cup E\cup F)\). Every point of \(R\) has Boolean active coordinates and exactly one neutral two, with its other neutral coordinates binary. The support is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^k\), every point has at most two coordinates equal to two, and its actual one-step core \(D_1\), defined below, is complete. No characterization of the individual extra roots in \(R\) is required.

For every \(\beta=(\gamma,\eta)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^L\), use the original law
$$
A=D\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^N,
\qquad w_{(y,t)}=\exp(-\gamma\cdot y-\eta\cdot t),
\qquad Z=\sum_{x\in D}w_x,
\qquad p_{(x,0)}=w_x/Z.
$$
Write \(p_x=p_{(x,0)}\) solely as an abbreviation. Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_p(z)&=\inf_{\substack{H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ closed affine halfspace}\\z\in H}}
\sum_{u\in A\cap H}p_u,\\
M_3(p)&=\sum_{z\in A}p_z\tau_p(z)^3,\\
s_p(c)&=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D\\x+y=2c}}\min(p_x,p_y),
\qquad T(p)=\sum_{c\in D}p_c s_p(c)^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
The reflection sum is over ordered pairs, with the diagonal once. Halfspaces may be required to have nonzero normal. These definitions, the original normalization, and the embedding agree exactly with accepted fact f27ee487069e27e7. Uniformly over all \(\gamma\) and \(\eta\),
$$
M_3(p)\ge2^{-46}8^{-(k+1)},
\qquad T(p)\ge2^{-46}8^{-(k+1)}.
\tag{2}
$$

For every such field, define the actual and hypothetical full one-step cores and their weights by
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_1&=\left\lbrace x\in D:\#\lbrace j:x_j=2\rbrace\le1\right\rbrace,\\
D_1^{\mathrm{full}}&=\left\lbrace x\in\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^k:\#\lbrace j:x_j=2\rbrace\le1\right\rbrace,\\
W_1&=\sum_{x\in D_1}w_x,\qquad W_1^{\mathrm{full}}=\sum_{x\in D_1^{\mathrm{full}}}w_x,
\qquad \alpha=W_1/Z,\qquad \delta=W_1/W_1^{\mathrm{full}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hypothetical full-core points enter only \(W_1^{\mathrm{full}}\), never the original law.

For the following particular specialization, take \(m\ge4\), put
$$
S_b=\sum_{j=1}^m j b_j,\qquad n_{(b,i)}=4^{S_b+2i},\qquad L=\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}n_q,
$$
and partition all neutral indices into disjoint groups of these sizes. These groups satisfy the hypotheses above, and in this specialization \(R=\varnothing\). Choose the field
$$
\gamma_i=i\log4\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \eta_h=0\quad(1\le h\le L).
\tag{3}
$$
All its activities are at most one. Then \(L\ge16Q\) and
$$
\alpha\le\frac4Q,\qquad \delta\le\frac4L,
\qquad
1+\frac m2-\frac1{10\,2^m}
\le\frac{|D_1|}{2^k}\le1+\frac m2.
\tag{4}
$$
In particular \(\alpha,\delta\to0\) and \(|D_1|/2^k\sim m/2\) as \(m\to\infty\).

For any nonempty actual subset \(V\subseteq D\), in each parity class meeting \(V\) list its distinct represented energies \(e_x=-\log p_x\) increasingly as \(e_{c,1},\ldots,e_{c,d_c}\), and put
$$
\kappa_{\mathrm{par},V}(p)
=\sum_{c:V_c\ne\varnothing}\left[1+\sum_{j=1}^{d_c-1}
\tanh\left(\frac{e_{c,j+1}-e_{c,j}}4\right)\right],
\qquad V_c=\lbrace x\in V:x\equiv c\pmod2\rbrace.
$$
This is exactly the retained capacity \(\mathcal L_V(p)\) of accepted fact 73f9d0102f4f4461: substitute \(A=D\times\lbrace0\rbrace\) for its support and \(N=k+1\) for its ambient dimension, and identify its probability at \((x,0)\) with the original \(p_x\) here. Its kernel weight \(w=p\) is the normalized original probability, not the unnormalized \(w_x\) here. The final zero coordinate adds no occupied parity classes. No conditioning on \(V\) is performed. At the field (3), uniformly over every actual subset,
$$
p(V)\ge\frac12
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{par},V}(p)}{2^k}\ge\frac{9m}{160}.
\tag{5}
$$
Hence no absolute bound \(C2^k\) for this capacity can always be attained by a subset of original mass at least \(1/2\), even with all activities at most one.

At the same field, set \(n=4^{m(m+3)/2}\). The actual original moments satisfy
$$
8^kT(p)\ge\frac{n^2 8^m}{1024Q^4},
\qquad
8^kM_3(p)\ge\frac{n^2 8^m}{8192Q^4}.
\tag{6}
$$
Both lower bounds tend to infinity, and therefore so do both original cubics multiplied by \(8^{k+1}\). Some actual centers also satisfy \(2^N\tau_p((c,0))\ge n/(4m)\).
